fullParagraphs: The overturning of the mandate in the Gokul Dairy cooperative is disturbing

Amid a nationwide outcry over electoral malpractices, with fresh evidence emerging every day, the BJP government in Maharashtra has gone a step further in overturning a popular mandate through an executive fiat. It approved changing the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act through an ordinance on November 4 — which the Governor promulgated on November 6 — with the immediate effect of facilitating the takeover of the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union, popularly known as Gokul Dairy , by the BJP and its allies. A Congress-led panel won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the board of the cooperative on October 19. Gokul, which is one of Maharashtra’s most influential cooperative institutions, has an annual turnover of around ₹4,000 crore and is linked to several lakh milk producers in western Maharashtra. The BJP had set its eyes on the cooperative sector as yet another arena of its political dominance, creating a Ministry of Cooperation under Home Minister Amit Shah. While that plan of controlling cooperatives continues to play out through various means, the overturning of an election clearly won by the Congress-led Opposition marks a new level of brazenness by the BJP, and of the impunity its actions continue to receive from the judiciary.

The Congress-backed Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi, led by Satej Patil, won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the Gokul board. On October 29, the election of the chairman was deadlocked after the BJP-allied members did not participate, and the meeting fell short of the required quorum of 14 members. The directors allied to the Congress and its partners subsequently declared Shashikant Patil Chuyekar as chairman, but the administration refused to recognise the election as quorum requirements had not been met. The amendment made through the ordinance allowed the government to nominate five directors to certain large cooperative institutions, with four nominees receiving voting rights. To be sure, four were nominated immediately to the Gokul board, and they voted with the BJP and its partners to elect a chairman on November 10 . The mandate of the cooperative’s members had been 13-12 in favour of the Congress and its allies, but it turned 16-13 in favour of the BJP and its partners, with the appointment of members with voting rights by the State government. Those defeated approached the Bombay High Court on November 9 to restrain the government-nominated directors from voting, but the High Court did not grant that relief. The diffidence of the judiciary in intervening in favour of democratic principles is turning out to be a matter of concern . The overturning of the popular mandate in Gokul Dairy cannot be seen as an isolated incident. It is yet another instance in a troubling pattern of state power silencing the people’s choice.

articles.title: Visions of the future: On this year’s Booker Prize
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society

A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.

One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic , the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion . Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything , with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.

• A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.
• One of the judges said she had also sought a book “only a human being could write”, but defending a novel for its ability to thumb its nose at the machines is unfair to the literary enterprise and betrays a wider public anxiety about AI, especially over the lack of consensus about its proper place in society. OpenAI has been aggravating these deliberations among mathematicians by using its machines to make headway, in record time, on problems that have been unsolved for decades, without also contributing to mathematical education and research. Anthropic , the American company known for its Claude AI model, has announced its IPO with a surprising proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion . Since much of this is pegged on speculative future demand for AI services, the same absence of consensus leaves room for investors to imagine an enormous market for Anthropic’s products and invest to help the company realise them, thus narrowing the space for society to deliberate on all competing visions of the future. And while The End of Everything , with its philosophy of pragmatic absurdism, offers poor guidance on how to keep that space open, doing so ultimately remains one of the most important unfinished tasks before the world today.

articles.title: Caste and class: On OBC reservation
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Exclusion of creamy layer is essential, but must be done consistently

If public resources are to dismantle both caste hierarchy and class inequality, OBC reservation should resist the notion that caste disadvantage makes economic differences among OBC families irrelevant. The ‘creamy layer’ rules are responsible for identifying those OBC members who have advanced sufficiently to no longer require affirmative action. However, the government has implemented them inconsistently. The Supreme Court in March corrected one inconsistency, that the government cannot hold the salary alone of an OBC candidate’s parent as evidence of social advancement. In Indra Sawhney (1992) , the Court upheld the government’s 27% reservation for OBC candidates in central government services if it also excluded economically advanced sections, i.e., the creamy layer, among OBCs. Following the equivalence requirement issued in 1993, the Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) issued a “clarification” in 2004 that the government used, from around 2015, to deny dozens of OBC candidates who had cleared the Civil Services Examination their benefits because their parents’ salaries exceeded the official threshold due to pay revisions that did not always reflect changes in occupational status. The Cabinet also approved equivalence guidelines in 2017 but a parliamentary committee criticised it over a number of issues.

In Rohith Nathan (2026) , the Court rightly rejected the government’s use of the 2004 “clarification” to arbitrarily exclude OBC candidates based on their parents’ salaries alone. However, the government stalled service allocations following the 2025 examination and appealed that retrospectively applying the ruling would create administrative chaos. On November 6, the Court conceded that it had not asked the government to reopen completed selections, as it could set workers against one another while leaving government misapplication unaddressed. A proactive policy is essential now as the government must create supernumerary posts for legitimate claimants and apply the 1993 rules to pending allocations without vouchsafing these remedies for only those who can afford litigation. Access to public employment continues to be grossly unequal: per the 2024-25 DoPT Annual Report, OBC representation in central government employment was 26.3% but declined steadily towards higher positions. As the Justice G. Rohini Commission also indicated, the benefits of reservation are distributed unevenly among OBC communities. However, the report, submitted in 2023, is still not in the public domain. The coming Census includes caste enumeration but policymakers also need data on each caste’s education, occupations, assets, and landholdings. Defending redistribution among caste groups while ignoring major inequalities within them, and constraining OBC reservation assuming relatively more high-income families capture the benefits without first establishing the extent and the causes are equally difficult to justify.

articles.title: Without any rationale: On the disbanding of the Justice Kurian Joseph Committee
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India’s federal structure could have benefited from the Kurian Committee

By abruptly disbanding the Justice Kurian Joseph Committee on Union-State Relations and handing over its task to the Tamil Nadu State Law Commission, the C. Joseph Vijay government appears to have succumbed to the political impulse to reverse earlier decisions rather than being guided by any compelling rationale or necessity. This gains credence from the very grounds cited. The committee executed its mandate with scholarly rigour, seen in Part I of its report that was submitted to the then M.K. Stalin government in February. Citing the Committee’s basic character of being a “non-statutory body” is unconvincing, particularly when the Law Commission itself is established only through “executive order”. There is also no public evidence of State Law Commissions having examined or addressed issues concerning Union-State relations. The mandate “to suggest ways and means for the inter-State relations and Centre-State relations”, constitutes only one part of the broader terms of reference of the State Law Commission, reconstituted in August. Given the commission’s wider responsibilities, successive State governments had constituted high-level committees to examine conflicts involving Concurrent List subjects and recommend specific remedies. It is through such recommendations that Tamil Nadu enacted certain pieces of legislation to overcome limitations imposed by central laws, including the provision of horizontal reservation in professional course admissions for disadvantaged students. Therefore, the State’s other argument of “similarity or overlap” in the “nature and scope of the functions” entrusted to the Committee and the Commission, does not withstand close scrutiny.

In September, Leader of the Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin, had flagged an attempt to “paralyse” the Committee’s functioning . A fair assessment of the Committee’s Part I Report reveals the breadth and depth of its dispassionate examination of issues, including State autonomy, delimitation, and the office of the Governor. Parties, barring the BJP, had largely welcomed the report. Interestingly, its contents are not even remotely at odds with the broad public ideological positioning of Mr. Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam on State rights. Besides, Prof. M. Naganathan, the Committee’s only member with an overt political association, had already resigned. The government would do well to rethink and allow it to complete its work. This would strengthen the political endeavour towards evolving a more balanced federal governance structure, facilitating harmonious Centre-State relations.

articles.summary: India’s federal structure could have benefited from the Kurian Committee
articles.keyPoints:
• India’s federal structure could have benefited from the Kurian Committee
• By abruptly disbanding the Justice Kurian Joseph Committee on Union-State Relations and handing over its task to the Tamil Nadu State Law Commission, the C. Joseph Vijay government appears to have succumbed to the political impulse to reverse earlier decisions rather than being guided by any compelling rationale or necessity. This gains credence from the very grounds cited. The committee executed its mandate with scholarly rigour, seen in Part I of its report that was submitted to the then M.K. Stalin government in February. Citing the Committee’s basic character of being a “non-statutory body” is unconvincing, particularly when the Law Commission itself is established only through “executive order”. There is also no public evidence of State Law Commissions having examined or addressed issues concerning Union-State relations. The mandate “to suggest ways and means for the inter-State relations and Centre-State relations”, constitutes only one part of the broader terms of reference of the State Law Commission, reconstituted in August. Given the commission’s wider responsibilities, successive State governments had constituted high-level committees to examine conflicts involving Concurrent List subjects and recommend specific remedies. It is through such recommendations that Tamil Nadu enacted certain pieces of legislation to overcome limitations imposed by central laws, including the provision of horizontal reservation in professional course admissions for disadvantaged students. Therefore, the State’s other argument of “similarity or overlap” in the “nature and scope of the functions” entrusted to the Committee and the Commission, does not withstand close scrutiny.
• In September, Leader of the Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin, had flagged an attempt to “paralyse” the Committee’s functioning . A fair assessment of the Committee’s Part I Report reveals the breadth and depth of its dispassionate examination of issues, including State autonomy, delimitation, and the office of the Governor. Parties, barring the BJP, had largely welcomed the report. Interestingly, its contents are not even remotely at odds with the broad public ideological positioning of Mr. Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam on State rights. Besides, Prof. M. Naganathan, the Committee’s only member with an overt political association, had already resigned. The government would do well to rethink and allow it to complete its work. This would strengthen the political endeavour towards evolving a more balanced federal governance structure, facilitating harmonious Centre-State relations.

articles.title: Cracker conundrum: On need for strict enforcement of cracker ban
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Any regulation of crackers needs strict enforcement at all levels

The two Deepavali nights following the Supreme Court’s (SC) temporary relaxation of the cracker ban , played out predictably. The Air Quality Index (AQI) in several north Indian cities — already ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ in the first week of November — was ‘severe’ on Deepavali night . Several air sensors — maintained by various organisations — reported PM2.5 in Delhi and its outskirts, exceeding 1,000 by Deepavali night. In this context, the SC’s order last week regarding crackers bears revisiting. While stating it was aware of the consequences of emissions from crackers, the Court has been waiting for quantitative evidence on the health and environmental effects of emissions from Deepavali celebrations. Such direct, causative evidence is almost impossible to furnish. Slackening winds and post-monsoon atmospheric dryness are known to trap the latent particulate matter from vehicles, industries, construction dust and stubble burning. Crackers are only an additional element that further degrades an already vitiated air. Delhi’s five-day average AQI rose from approximately 298 before Deepavali to 358 afterwards in 2024, 259 to 315 in 2025 and from 350 to 376 in 2026. While the timing of these spikes is consistent with a contribution from firecrackers, their precise share of overall pollution cannot be isolated from other emissions and meteorological influences. An absolute ban would encourage “illegal crackers from across the border,” the Court was told. Cracker season begins a fortnight before Deepavali and therefore an earlier decision by the Court regarding its permissibility would have given stockists time to better dispense ‘green’ crackers.

However, it is important to note that CSIR-NEERI, the developers of the products, underline that low-emission crackers — under stringent lab conditions — only reduce emissions by 30%–45%. These percentage reductions reveal nothing about gross particulate matter emissions. The post-Deepavali AQI is evidence of this. The Court acknowledges, but does not address, the immense implementation challenges in policing cracker sales and hyphenates crackers with religious observation but pays only lip service to provisions in the Constitution that say that religious customs cannot override considerations of health and life. Rather than wait for the week running up to Deepavali 2027, the Court must pronounce a final view on crackers and lay down the contours for the government to evolve a policy on limiting the manufacture, sale, and burning of crackers in a time-bound manner.

Editorial Context: Cracker conundrum: On need for strict enforcement of cracker ban. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

articles.title: Point of no return: On Israel’s next government
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Without peace, Israel risks descending into chaos

Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision to invite opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government reflects the real mandate of the October 27 legislative elections. While Mr. Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party finished second with 21 seats, behind Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud, which won 27, the former military chief, who campaigned on an anti-Netanyahu platform, has secured the support of 67 legislators in the 120-member Knesset. In Mr. Eisenkot’s own words, Israel risks “descending to dark places, to a point of no return”. But it is not yet clear what kind of a government Mr. Eisenkot is seeking to form. The opposition parties are split between a Jewish-led bloc with 48 MKs and an Arab-led bloc of 19 MKs. Arab parties have offered in-principle support for Mr. Eisenkot to keep Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition out of power. But what is not clear is whether they would be part of the government or offer outside support by allowing Mr. Eisenkot to run a minority government. Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s Jewish right-wing allies, such as Avigdor Lieberman, are opposed to joining hands with Arab parties. Mr. Eisenkot has now called for a unity government, appealing even to Likud and the far-right Religious Zionism, to join him.

But the challenges facing Israel’s next leader are formidable and immediate. Mr. Netanyahu’s unchecked militarism has deepened Israel’s international isolation, strained its relationship with the U.S., its most important patron and ally, and aggravated the security challenges it faces in its neighbourhood. At home, the surge of the far-right has further polarised society, while systemic violence against Palestinians has spread across the West Bank. Mr. Netanyahu’s response to these challenges has been to unleash more violence, which has only compounded Israel’s problems. If Mr. Eisenkot is serious about pulling Israel back from the point of no return, he must pursue a three-pronged approach. Firstly, he should form an Arab-Jewish unity government focused on healing the country’s internal wounds and bridging gaps between communities. Second, Israel’s deepening international isolation and increasingly negative public opinion around the world will begin to exact a heavy toll sooner rather than later. Tel Aviv must take urgent steps to restore its international standing. Third, Israel must reopen the path to peace. The new government should initiate negotiations with the Palestinians under international mediation, crack down on settler violence, pull back from Gaza and reaffirm its commitment to the two-state solution. Without peace, Israel risks continuing to “descend to dark places”.
Editorial Context: Point of no return: On Israel’s next government. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

articles.title: CPI seeks probe into ‘poll discrepancies’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Ramakrishna demands resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing him of favouring BJP and RSS

The Communist Party of India (CPI) has demanded a comprehensive probe by the Union government into alleged discrepancies between votes polled and counted in the Lok Sabha elections, as highlighted by investigative journalism organisation, The Reporters' Collective.

Addressing the media at Dasari Bhavan here on Thursday, CPI national secretary K. Ramakrishna and State secretary Gujjula Eswaraiah alleged that the findings raised serious questions about the integrity of the electoral process.

Mr. Ramakrishna said the organisation had analysed data from around 530 Lok Sabha constituencies and reported discrepancies in Maharashtra, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir. He demanded that the Election Commission of India's internal reports be made public and subjected to scrutiny.

Mr. Ramakrishna demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing him of favouring the BJP and the RSS. He questioned the addition of 50 to 60 million voters ahead of the Maharashtra Assembly elections, despite the BJP's setback in the preceding parliamentary elections.

He said the CPI national executive would meet in New Delhi on November 16 and 17 to discuss organising a nationwide movement along with INDIA bloc partners, mass organisations and civil rights groups.

Mr. Eswaraiah said victories secured unanimously in several rural and urban local bodies could not be celebrated if they were allegedly achieved through administrative pressure. Free elections and genuine voter participation were essential for democratic legitimacy, he said.
He announced a State-wide agitation against the proposed privatisation, warning that the decision would invite public opposition.

The CPI leaders criticised the Centre and the State government for “failing to provide adequate relief to farmers and people affected by drought and successive cyclones”. They said several villages continued to face power outages even 14 to 15 days after the cyclones made landfall.

They expressed concern over rising prices of rice, pulses, tomatoes, onions, garlic and ginger, alleging that the governments had failed to intervene effectively in the market. CPI State Secretariat member Donepudi Shankar was also present.

articles.title: Medical examination of recaptured prisoners, allegedly thrashed by Theni jail warders, confirms injuries
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Justices A.D. Jagadish Chandira and B. Karthikeyan of the Madras High Court direct government doctors to provide medical treatment to the injured prisoners

A medical examination ordered by the Madras High Court with respect to four out of 17 recaptured prisoners, who escaped from Theni district jail on October 26, 2026, and allegedly thrashed by the warders after their recapture within two days, has revealed that they are suffering from multiple injuries.

A Division Bench of Justices A.D. Jagadish Chandira and B. Karthikeyan were told that the medical examination of three prisoners, now shifted to the Salem central prison, and the fourth prisoner lodged at Palayamkottai central prison, by government doctors had confirmed the injuries sustained by them.

The judges decided to take a further call on the issue after receipt of a report from the Tamil Nadu State Legal Services Authority (TNSLSA) on the inquiry that it had initiated with respect to allegations of the 17 prisoners having escaped from the prison only because of torture and ill-treatment by the warders.

They directed the High Court Registry to list a writ petition filed by K. articles.title: Karnataka targets 24 GW power capacity in five years; plans over ₹3 lakh crore investment
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Global Investors Meet is scheduled to be held in Bengaluru between April 20 and 22, 2027

Karnataka is targeting an installed power capacity of around 24 GW over the next five years, requiring investments of more than ₹3 lakh crore in the power sector alone, indicated Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar.

The Chief Minister on Thursday said the State was looking to expand its energy infrastructure alongside industrial growth, with a focus on renewable energy and sustainable development. The State was also expanding its renewable energy capacity, emphasising the need to align industrial development with sustainability, he said, adding that his government’s ambition was not merely to make Karnataka an industrial hub but also a clean industrial hub.

Addressing an audience of investors, potential investors, diplomats, and trade bodies at the curtain-raiser for the Global Investors Meet, scheduled to be held in Bengaluru between April 20 and 22, 2027, Mr. Shivakumar said the proposed investment would be a key component of Karnataka’s next phase of economic expansion.
Recalling the State’s pioneering role in electricity generation, he pointed out that Asia’s first hydroelectric power generation facility was established at Shivanasamudra in 1902.

Seeking to position the State as a preferred investment destination, he said Karnataka’s strengths extended beyond information technology and biotechnology to aerospace, semiconductors, machine tools and electric mobility.

The government, he further said, was attempting to address regional imbalances in industrial development by encouraging investments outside Bengaluru. Industrial parks, roads, logistics facilities and airport connectivity were being strengthened in cities such as Mysuru, Mangaluru, Hubballi, Tumakuru and Kalaburagi.
Mr. Shivakumar said the government already met over 200 investors over five to six months and was committed to resolving bottlenecks in project implementation.

Commenting on the scope of aerospace and defence industries, he said the sector had attracted investments exceeding ₹60,000 crore and generated around 60,000 jobs, adding the government was looking to create another 5 lakh employment opportunities.

Minister for Large and Medium Industries and Infrastructure Development M.B. Patil said that Karnataka converted around 65% of the manufacturing investment commitments received at its previous Global Investors Meet into projects on the ground, with several companies having moved from approvals and land allotments to construction and commercial operations, .

Mr. Patil said the State had secured investment commitments of about ₹10.27 lakh crore at the previous summit, adding that the government was now focusing on translating proposals into factories and employment.

articles.title: Vizag CII Summit: ReNew to invest ₹80,000 crore in green data centre, solar manufacturing in Andhra Pradesh
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Investments include a ₹67,000-crore Green Hyperscale Data Centre in Anakapalli, ₹11,000-crore polysilicon and metallurgical silicon manufacturing facilities in Anakapalli and Nellore; and ₹1,500-crore permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli

ReNew Energy Global Plc, a leading decarbonisation solutions company, has announced fresh investments of approximately ₹80,000 crore in Andhra Pradesh, spanning digital infrastructure and clean energy manufacturing.

The investments include a ₹67,000-crore 1 GW Green Hyperscale Data Centre in Anakapalli, ₹11,000-crore polysilicon and metallurgical silicon manufacturing facilities in Anakapalli and Nellore; and a ₹1,500-crore permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli.
Besides, the company will set up the ReNew Centre for Technical Excellence in Visakhapatnam under the PM SETU Scheme.
The announcements were made at the CII Partnership Summit 2026 held in Visakhapatnam under the leadership of Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu, and in the presence of IT & HRD Minister Nara Lokesh.
Together, the investments expand ReNew’s presence across digital infrastructure, renewable energy, clean energy manufacturing and skilling, deepening its long-term partnership with Andhra Pradesh.

Commenting on the proposals, Sumant Sinha, Founder-Chairman and CEO of ReNew, said that Andhra Pradesh was emerging as an important destination for India’s industrial and digital growth, and ReNew’s investments would bring together two of India’s biggest growth opportunities, digitalisation and decarbonisation, while strengthening clean energy manufacturing, infrastructure and skills.

ReNew was working in tandem with the Andhra Pradesh government towards achieving the State’s target of generating 78.50 GW of solar, 35 GW of wind power capacity, and 25 GWh of battery energy storage systems, Mr. Sinha said.
Company’s co-founder Vaishali Nigam Sinha and CEO (Solar Manufacturing) Sanjay Varghese were present.

📰 Vizag CII Summit: ReNew to invest ₹80,000 crore in green data centre, solar manufacturing in Andhra Pradesh

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes

Investments include a ₹67,000-crore Green Hyperscale Data Centre in Anakapalli, ₹11,000-crore polysilicon and metallurgical silicon manufacturing facilities in Anakapalli and Nellore; and ₹1,500-crore permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli

ReNew Energy Global Plc, a leading decarbonisation solutions company, has announced fresh investments of approximately ₹80,000 crore in Andhra Pradesh, spanning digital infrastructure and clean energy manufacturing.

The investments include a ₹67,000-crore 1 GW Green Hyperscale Data Centre in Anakapalli, ₹11,000-crore polysilicon and metallurgical silicon manufacturing facilities in Anakapalli and Nellore; and a ₹1,500-crore permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli.

Besides, the company will set up the ReNew Centre for Technical Excellence in Visakhapatnam under the PM SETU Scheme.

The announcements were made at the CII Partnership Summit 2026 held in Visakhapatnam under the leadership of Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu, and in the presence of IT & HRD Minister Nara Lokesh.

Together, the investments expand ReNew’s presence across digital infrastructure, renewable energy, clean energy manufacturing and skilling, deepening its long-term partnership with Andhra Pradesh.

Commenting on the proposals, Sumant Sinha, Founder-Chairman and CEO of ReNew, said that Andhra Pradesh was emerging as an important destination for India’s industrial and digital growth, and ReNew’s investments would bring together two of India’s biggest growth opportunities, digitalisation and decarbonisation, while strengthening clean energy manufacturing, infrastructure and skills.

ReNew was working in tandem with the Andhra Pradesh government towards achieving the State’s target of generating 78.50 GW of solar, 35 GW of wind power capacity, and 25 GWh of battery energy storage systems, Mr. Sinha said.

Company’s co-founder Vaishali Nigam Sinha and CEO (Solar Manufacturing) Sanjay Varghese were present.

articles.title: India records 38% drop in TB mortality since 2015: WHO report
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: World Health Organization’s Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 showed a total of 1.13 million people died from tuberculosis last year

India has seen a 38% reduction in tuberculosis (TB) mortality since 2015, compared to a global average of 35%, and a 94% treatment success rate among patients with drug-susceptible TB, according to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report 2026.
Last year, the South-East Asia Region recorded the largest number of new TB cases (35%), followed by the Western Pacific Region (27%) and the African Region (25%).

Around 88% of new TB cases occurred in 30 countries. India (about a quarter), Indonesia (10%), the Philippines (6.8%), China (6.5%), Pakistan (6.4%), Nigeria (4.9%), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (3.9%) and Bangladesh (3.7%) accounted for about a q of the global total.

Globally, about 50% of people treated for TB and their households face total costs (direct medical expenditures, non-medical expenditures, and indirect costs such as income losses) that are catastrophic (greater than 20% of total household income).

People with compromised immune systems, such as those living with HIV, undernutrition or diabetes, or people who use tobacco have a higher risk of falling ill. An estimated 9.6 lakh new TB cases were attributable to undernutrition, 9.2 lakh to diabetes, 7.3 lakh to alcohol use disorders, 6.9 lakh to smoking and 5.5 lakh to HIV infection.

The report showed a total of 1.13 million people died from TB in 2025. Globally, TB is the world’s leading cause of death from a single infectious agent. Last year, an estimated 10.6 million people fell ill with TB worldwide, including 5.7 million men, 3.7 million women and 1.2 million children.

Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) remains a public health crisis and a health security threat. Only about two in five people with drug-resistant TB received treatment in 2025. Global efforts to combat TB have saved an estimated 86 million lives since 2000.
Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria that most often affects the lungs. It spreads through the air when people with TB cough, sneeze or spit. TB is preventable and curable.
Between December 7, 2024 and November 8, 2026, the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan achieved significant progress, identifying and bringing over 25 crore individuals within the scope of screening activities.

“India’s reduction in TB mortality has been the result of interventions under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), including proactive case finding including use of AI-enabled X-rays, rapid diagnostics, prompt treatment initiation, differentiated TB care, and nutritional support through the Nikshay Poshan Yojana and Nikshay Mitra initiative. These interventions were supported by AI tools for identification of hotspots, prediction of high-risk TB cases prone for adverse outcomes, Khushi – AI Chatbot & Avatar Videobot, etc.,” the Union Health Ministry statement said.

articles.title: CAG widens purview of power sector audit, starting with DISCOMs; consumer satisfaction in focus
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Officials stated that DISCOMs would be evaluated for their performance over a five-year period, following by transmission, generation, renewable energy and RDSS.

The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is undertaking a comprehensive audit of the power sector, beginning with distribution companies (discoms), where consumer satisfaction, power trading and financial sustainability emerging as key focus areas.

The exercise will subsequently cover transmission, generation, renewable energy and the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), with each segment’s operational and financial performance being assessed over the preceding five years, according to officials familiar with the development.

Discoms will be the first to be audited, with the ongoing phase covering their performance between FY21 and FY26. As many as 39 discoms across the country, along with five departmental undertakings, will be assessed. Privately owned discoms, however, will remain outside the scope of the exercise.
The audit commenced in July this year, with the report expected to be finalised around the middle of the next financial year. The audit of the transmission segment is scheduled to begin with FY27.
Moving beyond conventional financial and operational assessments, the CAG has directed auditors to engage directly with electricity consumers, local experts and influential groups..
“We told our auditors that it (the audit) must not be limited to a stakeholder consultation exercise, we must engage with consumers of electricity,” an official said.
The exercise will capture the experiences of around 10,000 consumers across industrial, agricultural and domestic categories, with particular emphasis on the reliability and quality of power supply.

Power trading and procurement costs will constitute another major area of scrutiny. Officials pointed out that the share of short-term power procurement in states’ overall power purchase basket has risen from around 7-8% five years ago to nearly 14% currently, with power exchanges accounting for more than 56% of such transactions.
“Ultimately, the cost at which the power is purchased would impact the end consumer of the electricity, and it also impacts financials of the entities concerned,” officials said.

The audit will also examine key operational indicators, including aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses, billing and collection efficiency, alongside the financial health and long-term viability of discoms.

articles.title: Retail inflation crosses RBI’s upper limit for first time in two years, comes in at 6.1% in October 2026
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The Consumer Price Index saw almost all categories hit series highs as inflation spread across sectors of the economy

Retail inflation rose to 6.1% in October 2026, crossing the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) upper threshold for the first time in two years. The continued uptick in inflation, while driven by food and fuel prices, has now spread to nearly all sectors, data released by the government on Thursday shows.

The RBI targets an inflation rate of 4% with a comfort band of 2% higher or lower than figure. Inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) last crossed this upper threshold of 6% in October 2024, when it came in at 6.2%. Retail inflation in October 2026 was the highest since then.

The new series of the CPI, with a base year of 2024, has sectoral data that goes back to only January 2026, which means a historical analysis is possible only up to that point. Within that, the latest data shows inflation across most categories rose to series highs in October 2026.

“Although inflation remains predominantly supply-driven, stronger consumer demand pull associated with festive-season purchases may have added to price pressures, reinforcing the RBI’s decision to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%,” Pranjal Ghate, economist at Brickwork Ratings said, referring to the Monetary Policy Committee’s (MPC) latest decision in early October 2026.

The data shows that inflation in the food and beverages category rose sharply to 8.5% in October 2026, the highest in the series. Coupled with this, rising fuel prices meant that inflation in the transport category also rose to 5.8% in October, a series high.

As a result of accelerating food and transport prices, inflation in the restaurant and accommodation services category jumped to 10.1% in October, the first time it has come in at double-digits in the new series.
According to Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at the Bank of Baroda, some food prices could rise further in the coming months.

“The ongoing harvest prospects will throw more light on how food prices behave,” Mr. Sabnavis said. “Area under cultivation was lower for rice, maize, oilseeds, cotton and sugarcane. It has also been reported that pulses production, especially tur, could be lower this time, which can lead to a spike in prices.”
Apart from food and fuel, the data shows that other aspects of day-to-day life have also seen prices rising at a faster pace.

Clothing and footwear, for example, saw inflation coming in at nearly 5% in October 2026 — the highest in this series — from 3.9% in the previous month. The ‘furnishings, household equipment, and routine household maintenance’ category saw inflation quicken to 3.9% in October, also a series high.

articles.title: Why RBI wants to cap select overseas remittances at ₹50 Lakh to save rupees | Explained

fullParagraphs: The RBI has reportedly proposed a ₹50 lakh sub-limit within the ₹2,50,000 annual Liberalised Remittance Scheme cap to curb dollar outflows and protect the rupee

The story so far: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reportedly proposed to the Ministry of Finance tightening the limits of the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), in an attempt likely aimed at preventing a massive outflow of dollars from India. Under the current structure, Indian residents can remit up to $250,000 (over ₹2 crore) in a financial year for purposes such as travel, education, medical treatment, and overseas investments.

The LRS is a scheme under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), introduced by the RBI in 2004. It covers both capital account and current account transactions. Under the capital account, transactions are permitted for opening overseas foreign currency bank accounts, purchasing property, extending interest-free loans of up to one year, and investing in foreign equity, mutual funds, and listed debt securities.

articles.title: Moody’s ups India’s FY27 growth estimate to 7% on broad-based momentum
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Robust consumption, improving investment dynamics and strong macroeconomic fundamentals imply that the economy appears well positioned to sustain growth near 7% over the medium term, Moody's said

Moody's Ratings on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) said the Indian economy is expected to grow at a higher rate of 7 per cent in the current fiscal, led by broad-based economic momentum and energy supply shock resilience.

In its Global Macro Outlook 2027-28, Moody's, however, said that near-term risks to growth persist as household consumption remains vulnerable to “intensifying and broadening price pressures”, with headline inflation close to the upper end of the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) 2-6% target range, while a deficient southwest monsoon and strengthening El Nino conditions will weigh on agricultural output and rural demand.
“India's broad-based economic momentum and demonstrated resilience to the energy supply shock warrant upward revisions to our 2026-27 growth forecasts to 7% from 6.5%,” it said.
Robust consumption, improving investment dynamics and strong macroeconomic fundamentals imply that the economy appears well positioned to sustain growth near 7% over the medium term, Moody's said.
A sustained private investment boom that materially boosts manufacturing, employment and productivity could lift growth rates above Moody's baseline projections.
“With the RBI on track to raise rates further, tighter monetary policy could delay the recovery in private investment,” Moody's added.

India has adjusted to the energy price shock better than previously assumed, helped by its ability to diversify crude and gas supplies and buffer consumers from the immediate price impact through state-backed oil marketing companies and tax cuts.

India is also home to the world's largest single-site refining complex, and its large and sophisticated refining capacity has helped limit fuel supply disruptions while supporting its role as a major exporter of refined petroleum products, Moody's added.

“High frequency indicators, including robust capital goods production and imports, accelerating industrial credit growth and rising capacity utilisation, suggest that India may be at the cusp of a new private capex cycle after several years of corporate and banking- sector balance sheet repair,” the U.S.-based agency said.

Broader economic activity also remains solid amid expanding manufacturing and services purchasing manager indexes and double-digit year-on-year growth in goods and services tax revenue, vehicle sales and merchandise exports, it added.

articles.title: Industry seeks LTCG, STT cuts in Budget 2027; MSME relief also on wish list
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Several industry bodies have been meeting top officials of the Finance Ministry as part of the annual pre-Budget consultation process

Several industry bodies have recommended to the Ministry of Finance that the upcoming Budget 2027 should rationalise the Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax rate on equities and reduce the rate of the Securities Transaction Tax (STT).

Officials in the Finance Ministry, including Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Revenue Secretary Arvind Shrivastava, have been conducting their pre-Budget consultative meetings, during which they met the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PHDCCI), and the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (ASSOCHAM), among others.

One of the most-cited requests from the industry was the rationalisation of LTCG on equities. In Budget 2026, the Centre removed the 12.5% LTCG tax in the government securities market for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) alongside other measures including reforms under the Fully Accessible Route (FAR).

Currently, foreign and domestic investors have to pay 12.5% tax on the sale of equities on gains exceeding Rs 1.25 lakh per annum on listed shares. The Centre has held several meetings with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and other industry players.

“Removing the LTCG levy would raise post-tax returns and close a gap with Korea, Taiwan and Brazil,” Rakesh Nangia, chairman of task force on International Taxes at ASSOCHAM said. “The debt market is a useful precedent, which after the G-sec relief, saw FPI inflows rise to about $9 billion in June-July.”

The PHDCCI has requested that the government abolish LTCG tax on equity investments, reduce the short-term capital gains (STCG) tax rate from 20% to 10%, and lower STT rates “to encourage long-term investment and improve India’s capital market competitiveness”.

In its representation to Ms. Sitharaman, FICCI highlighted the fact that foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have withdrawn about Rs 3.08 lakh crore during the year. It added that capital gains tax, which is charged over and above the STT, erodes returns from equities, and needs a review to make India a more attractive place to invest.

However, other market players highlight that the revenue loss incurred from the removal of LTCG could be negated through a hike in STT. According to estimates by SBI Research, the removal of LTCG would result in a revenue loss of Rs 40,000-50,000 crore for FY28.

One of the key frictions for FPIs underscored by industry bodies and equity analysts is the computation of the tax. Under Income-Tax Act, the calculation of the LTCG is in the Indian rupee. The challenge arises due to currency depreciation as against the investor’s base currency during the holding period, due to which investors are still liable to pay tax even when net returns in dollar terms are flat or even negative. This issue is currently under examination.

VK Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Financial Services also cautioned against selective relief, noting that abolishing LTCG solely for FPIs would be discriminatory against domestic retail and direct equity investors who remain subject to the 12.5% tax. He urged any tax relief must apply equally across the board to ensure a level playing field.

📈 Economic, Banking & Finance 📅 10 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 4 Min Read

📰 Industry seeks LTCG, STT cuts in Budget 2027; MSME relief also on wish list

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance

Several industry bodies have been meeting top officials of the Finance Ministry as part of the annual pre-Budget consultation process

Several industry bodies have recommended to the Ministry of Finance that the upcoming Budget 2027 should rationalise the Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax rate on equities and reduce the rate of the Securities Transaction Tax (STT).

Officials in the Finance Ministry, including Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Revenue Secretary Arvind Shrivastava, have been conducting their pre-Budget consultative meetings, during which they met the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PHDCCI), and the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (ASSOCHAM), among others.

One of the most-cited requests from the industry was the rationalisation of LTCG on equities. In Budget 2026, the Centre removed the 12.5% LTCG tax in the government securities market for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) alongside other measures including reforms under the Fully Accessible Route (FAR).

Currently, foreign and domestic investors have to pay 12.5% tax on the sale of equities on gains exceeding Rs 1.25 lakh per annum on listed shares. The Centre has held several meetings with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and other industry players.

“Removing the LTCG levy would raise post-tax returns and close a gap with Korea, Taiwan and Brazil,” Rakesh Nangia, chairman of task force on International Taxes at ASSOCHAM said. “The debt market is a useful precedent, which after the G-sec relief, saw FPI inflows rise to about $9 billion in June-July.”

The PHDCCI has requested that the government abolish LTCG tax on equity investments, reduce the short-term capital gains (STCG) tax rate from 20% to 10%, and lower STT rates “to encourage long-term investment and improve India’s capital market competitiveness”.

In its representation to Ms. Sitharaman, FICCI highlighted the fact that foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have withdrawn about Rs 3.08 lakh crore during the year. It added that capital gains tax, which is charged over and above the STT, erodes returns from equities, and needs a review to make India a more attractive place to invest.

However, other market players highlight that the revenue loss incurred from the removal of LTCG could be negated through a hike in STT. According to estimates by SBI Research, the removal of LTCG would result in a revenue loss of Rs 40,000-50,000 crore for FY28.

One of the key frictions for FPIs underscored by industry bodies and equity analysts is the computation of the tax. Under Income-Tax Act, the calculation of the LTCG is in the Indian rupee. The challenge arises due to currency depreciation as against the investor’s base currency during the holding period, due to which investors are still liable to pay tax even when net returns in dollar terms are flat or even negative. This issue is currently under examination.

VK Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Financial Services also cautioned against selective relief, noting that abolishing LTCG solely for FPIs would be discriminatory against domestic retail and direct equity investors who remain subject to the 12.5% tax. He urged any tax relief must apply equally across the board to ensure a level playing field.

fullParagraphs: The Russian President proposes a short-term ceasefire in a key frontline city in Donetsk; he also rules out agreeing to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine

Vladimir Putin indicated on Thursday (November 12, 2026) that Russia will not compromise on its hardline demands to end the Ukraine offensive but offered a short-term ceasefire in a key frontline city in Donetsk during a Kremlin meeting with U.S. envoys.

The Russian President said he would not water down his territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine that Russia claims to have annexed and ruled out agreeing to foreign peacekeeping troops being stationed in Ukraine — a deployment that he said would be a “continuation of war”.

The Americans, meanwhile, urged Mr. Putin to allow European representatives to sit at the table for the next round of talks.
Moscow has successfully managed to reframe the discussions on the war as part of a wider discussion about European security.

Usually held behind closed doors, the Kremlin chose to televise a lengthy opening exchange between Mr. Putin and the U.S. envoys.

articles.title: No need for Opposition approval to launch strikes, says Israel’s Katz
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot urged caretaker PM Netanyahu to show restraint, warning that force without a “direct and immediate threat” could have “disastrous consequences for Israeli democracy and citizens’ trust”

Israeli caretaker Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Thursday (November 12, 2026) that the outgoing coalition does not need permission from the opposition to decide on fresh military operations, following calls to show restraint.
“We do not need approval from the opposition or any legal authority” for the army to carry out strikes in any of the arenas where it operates, Mr. Katz wrote on X.

The leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, has called on caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to show restraint, warning that the use of force without a “direct and immediate threat” could have “disastrous consequences for Israeli democracy and for citizens’ trust”.
Mr. Netanyahu repeatedly threatened to resume the Iran war on the campaign trail for elections last month, warning of threats and even posting an image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv.

Mr. Katz said Thursday (November 12, 2026) that the outgoing coalition had “demonstrated resolve and sound judgment in dealing with Iran, in full coordination with the IDF — and that will remain the case now, as circumstances require”.
Mr. Netanyahu agreed to meet Thursday (November 12, 2026) with Mr. Eisenkot to discuss national security following the row over whether the outgoing government can resume the conflict.
In a short joint statement, Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Netanyahu said they would meet at the Prime Minister’s office for a briefing attended by Mr. Netanyahu’s military aide.
The announcement came a day after Mr. Eisenkot, who has a mandate to try to form a new government , accused Mr. Netanyahu of refusing to brief him, in what he called a deviation from protocol.

Avigdor Liberman, a key member of Mr. Eisenkot’s political bloc who has been named head of a parliamentary committee on foreign and defence affairs, also criticised Mr. Netanyahu on Thursday (November 12, 2026).

“I warn you: a caretaker government is not allowed to make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full consent of all security agencies,” said Liberman, a hawkish former aide to Mr. Netanyahu who has become a strident critic.

articles.title: Washington DC shooting: One dead, four people injured
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: A officer said the suspect shot himself while barricaded inside an apartment. He added that the man apparently had a dispute with the building’s homeowners association

Five people were shot on Thursday (November 12, 2026) in a trendy Washington, D.C., neighbourhood within walking distance of the White House, police said, and the suspected gunman shot himself as a swarm of officers responded to a nearby apartment building.
One victim died in the shooting, said Jeffrey Carroll, interim chief with the Metropolitan Police Department.
Carroll said the suspect shot himself while barricaded inside an apartment. He added that the man apparently had a dispute with the building’s homeowners association.

The shootings were reported in Logan Circle, about a mile north of the White House. Much of the block on 15th Street was cordoned off as police urged people to avoid the area, which includes a VIDA fitness centre, St. Luke’s Episcopal Church, residences and a Whole Foods supermarket. Schools were on lockdown.
Law enforcement SWAT teams and other officers had their guns drawn on the roof of an apartment building or on the ground below.

Authorities believe the suspect shot at least one person inside the gym before going outside and firing again, according to a law enforcement official who was not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.
Law enforcement agents believe the suspect shot another person in a parking garage elevator and then barricaded himself on the seventh floor of the building, the official said.
Witness James Spellman, who was at the gym, said there were about 50 people there around 8 am when the shooting began.
“Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” he said. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”
Spellman said he and others dashed out of the gym. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.

articles.title: Centre sanctions new roads, infrastructure along China’s border
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Indo-Tibetan Border Police sanctions the construction of 15 pedestrian suspension bridges and 18 log bridges in Arunachal Pradesh; CCS clears 26 new roads as part of ICBR-III

Amid continuing face-offs with the Chinese Army along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh since late July, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) has sanctioned the construction of new border infrastructure in the northeastern State, a senior government official told The Hindu .

Earlier, in February, the Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) had cleared the third phase of the Indo-China Border Roads (ICBR-III) project. Under the scheme, as many as 26 roads are to be constructed along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh, another government official said. The Union Government has not yet officially announced the ICBR-III project or publicly disclosed these details.
This is only the second time after the 2020 Galwan clashes in eastern Ladakh that a critical road infrastructure project has been sanctioned along the border with China.

The first phase of the ICBR was initiated in 2005 when it was decided that the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) would construct 27 priority roads with a total length of 608 km along the border with China.

The second phase of the ICBR, comprising 32 roads with a total length of 683 km, was approved on September 21, 2020, just months after 20 Indian soldiers were killed in violent clashes with the Chinese People’s Liberation Army in eastern Ladakh.

Since September, the ITBP has authorised the construction of 15 pedestrian suspension bridges and 18 log bridges in Upper Subansiri and Kurung Kumey districts, covering the areas bordering China in Arunachal Pradesh.

The project clearance came days after India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit from September 11 to 13 in New Delhi, which was attended by Chinese President Xi Jinping. Amid continuing face-offs with the Chinese Army along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh since late July, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) has sanctioned the construction of new border infrastructure in the northeastern State, a senior government official told The Hindu .

The first phase of the ICBR was initiated in 2005 when it was decided that the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) would construct 27 priority roads with a total length of 608 km along the border with China.

The second phase of the ICBR, comprising 32 roads with a total length of 683 km, was approved on September 21, 2020, just months after 20 Indian soldiers were killed in violent clashes with the Chinese People’s Liberation Army in eastern Ladakh.

articles.title: Amidst simmering tensions, India-Bangladesh consular dialogue postponed
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: This would have been the fifth such consular dialogue and the first after the August 2024 uprising; postponement due to tensions over former PM Hasina’s plan to return to Bangladesh next month

Days after Bangladesh’s deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requested Dhaka for a new passport and national identity card, the fifth India-Bangladesh consular dialogue that was scheduled to take place on November 17 and 18 has been postponed, a diplomatic source has confirmed.

The source indicated that the postponement of the dialogue was mainly on account of growing tensions in the bilateral relationship caused by Ms. Hasina’s announcement that she will return to Bangladesh next month.

The planned consular dialogue would have been the first such meeting between the two sides in more than two years. The last such dialogue was held in New Delhi on May 29, 2024, just over two months before the Hasina government fell in a youth-led uprising in Dhaka.

The consular dialogue was scheduled to be held in Dhaka at the level of Director Generals of the Foreign Ministries of both countries. The planned agenda included issues of border management, visa procedures, and the repatriation of citizens detained on both sides. The number of Indian visas issued was drastically reduced when tensions broke out in August 2024. According to sources, India has gradually increased the number of visas issued to travellers from Bangladesh in recent months, especially after the election of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in February this year.

The two countries started a consular dialogue in 2017 to “strengthen people-to-people contacts by having a regular channel of communication on consular, visa, and mutual legal assistance cooperation matters between India and Bangladesh.” Four rounds of consular dialogues were held during the rule of the Awami League in Dhaka. As per the Ministry of External Affairs, the fourth round held in May 2024 discussed issues like “visa matters, repatriation, Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty cases etc.”

Attempts at normalising the India-Bangladesh relationship in recent months have been hindered by Ms. Hasina’s presence in India, where she took refuge on August 5, 2024. On November 9 this year, a London-based legal firm representing Ms. Hasina wrote to the High Commission of Bangladesh in New Delhi requesting a new passport and the national ID card. “In view of the reported revocation of her existing Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card (NID) by the Interim Government and other authorities, I respectfully request that you take the necessary steps to issue a new Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card for our client,” said the letter sent by the law firm Matrix Chambers.

However, the Acting Foreign Minister of Bangladesh Humayun Kabir responded to this development by telling journalists that Bangladesh would not issue a passport to Ms. Hasina. Instead, he said, Dhaka would seek Ms. Hasina’s extradition under an “acceptable prisoner exchange process”, adding that such a handover would have to be conducted carefully and under proper surveillance.

articles.title: ISRO successfully carries out ground static test of PSLV third stage
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The configuration of the third stage was revisited comprehensively with respect to the design margins, raw material acceptance criteria, assembly procedures, and the quality checks that were followed so far

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) which is looking to get its workhorse launcher, the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), back on track has successfully carried out the ground static test of the PSLV third stage (PS3) at the Static Test Facility in Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota on Thursday (November 12, 2026).

“Subsequent to the anomalies observed in the third stage of PSLV during the PSLV-C61/EOS-09 & PSLV-C62 / EOS-N1 missions, the configuration of the PS3 stage was revisited comprehensively with respect to the design margins, raw material acceptance criteria, assembly procedures, and the quality checks that were followed so far,” ISRO said.

“The configuration has been strengthened and essential improvements have been carried out in the nozzle configuration to improve design margins along with updated procedures in the acceptance of raw materials, assembly procedures and quality checks,” ISRO added.
It also said that the mechanical interfaces have been strengthened with redundancy in the sealing systems and adequacy of the design margins have been verified.

“The updates in assembly procedures and non-destructive tests (NDT) during the various phases of integration and transportation have been implemented and the new version of the PS3 solid motor stage is realised and tested successfully,” ISRO said.
Based on the detailed analysis and reviews of the test data, the space agency said further tests are planned.

The configuration of the third stage was revisited comprehensively with respect to the design margins, raw material acceptance criteria, assembly procedures, and the quality checks that were followed so far

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) which is looking to get its workhorse launcher, the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), back on track has successfully carried out the ground static test of the PSLV third stage (PS3) at the Static Test Facility in Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota on Thursday (November 12, 2026).

“Subsequent to the anomalies observed in the third stage of PSLV during the PSLV-C61/EOS-09 & PSLV-C62 / EOS-N1 missions, the configuration of the PS3 stage was revisited comprehensively with respect to the design margins, raw material acceptance criteria, assembly procedures, and the quality checks that were followed so far,” ISRO said.

“The configuration has been strengthened and essential improvements have been carried out in the nozzle configuration to improve design margins along with updated procedures in the acceptance of raw materials, assembly procedures and quality checks,” ISRO added.

It also said that the mechanical interfaces have been strengthened with redundancy in the sealing systems and adequacy of the design margins have been verified.

“The updates in assembly procedures and non-destructive tests (NDT) during the various phases of integration and transportation have been implemented and the new version of the PS3 solid motor stage is realised and tested successfully,” ISRO said.

Based on the detailed analysis and reviews of the test data, the space agency said further tests are planned.

articles.title: India undergoing massive transformation in renewable energy: Earthshot Prize CEO
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: “There is a race on right now. The first country that can have access to cheap, clean and abundant energy, is going to have a huge economic advantage. And India knows that,” says Jason Knauf

India is at the forefront of climate solutions, and its innovations have immediate global application, especially when it comes to issues such as heat stress, Earthshot Prize CEO Jason Knauf said. He was speaking with The Hindu on Thursday (November 12, 2026) on the background of the launch of the five-day Earthshot Prize summit, which will take place in Mumbai and Jaipur from November 13 to 17.

As COP31 gathers in Türkiye for climate negotiations, it is India and Mumbai which will send a message of climate solutions, he said. “There is a race going on right now. The first country that can have access to cheap, clean and abundant energy, is going to have a huge economic advantage. And I think, India knows that. Which is why so much is being done here to use the huge solar resource that India has,” he said.

Earthshot Prize is one of the world’s most prestigious environmental awards. It was founded by Prince William six years ago. This is the first time the awards are being held in India. Prince William will be in India for the events.

On Thursday (November 12, 2026), Mr. Knauf spoke about how India was an inspiration behind starting the award, why the awards are being held in India and particularly in Mumbai this year, and the lessons he has learnt during his stay in the country. Observing that India is undergoing a “massive transformation” about renewable energy, he said it had an advantage over other countries to bring in sustainable climate solutions. He said there was no debate between economic progress and environmental protection anymore. “What is good for the environment is good for business, and Indian companies are showing that,” Mr. Knauf said, adding that the past Indian winners had been able to raise $800 million in commercial international investment after winning the Earthshot Prize.
The Earthshot Prize is slated to make large announcements about two Indian finalists — Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and Mahila Housing Trust, in the coming week.

Mr. Knauf said climate action conversation needed to move beyond the ‘environment bubble’. Acknowledging India’s efforts in the conservation sector, he said it was important to showcase India’s optimism to the world. Adding that the inspiration behind the awards came from India too, he spoke of how the Prince of Wales saw environmental action during his visit to India in 2016, when he was inspired by the country’s approach towards working with nature.

“For a country that is on the frontline of the environmental issues despite having not caused them, people are more optimistic about their abilities to solve them, than many richer countries. That tells you something. We all have to learn from that example. We are happy that the Earthshot Prize is coming here to celebrate that Indian spirit for the whole world,” Mr. Knauf said. He added that Mumbai was chosen as it was the financial and entertainment capital of the country.

“Earthshot Prize is about getting out to people. We want to get out to investors, to corporate leaders. We also want to tap into the world of entertainment and sporting. Mumbai is the perfect place for that. It is the global capital for the financial sector and the entertainment world,” he said.

This year, Earthshot Prize ceremony will be held at an unprecedented scale, he said, adding that over 5,000 people would participate in the events which would draw people from different countries, and children from over 24 States of India. The event would be live telecast around 240 countries for the first time.

Asked about how he saw the climate challenge, Mr. Knauf said he was an eternal optimist. “At Earthshot, we have a simple equation — urgency + optimism = action. Anyone who wants to give up and be negative, that is a big threat to action. As big a threat as carbon emissions. Because the second we decide that the issues are too hard, then we look the other way. That is giving up, and particularly for the next generation that is coming, it is an unacceptable attitude,” he said.

The company’s board said Mr. Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while keeping her finance role, and the board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement.

Mr. Huang faced growing calls to resign after his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Late Wednesday (November 11, 2026), media reports said Mr. Huang had another extramarital affair with an Nvidia employee who reports to him.

articles.title: Study suggests not all obesity means ill-health
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The study follows a proposal last year from experts and medical organisations to move obesity diagnosis beyond just body mass index (BMI), based on a person’s weight and height, to include body fat and broader health

Only between a quarter and a third of people currently diagnosed with obesity should be considered as in poor health, according to a new study that joins calls to overhaul how the condition is diagnosed.

The study, published in Nature on Wednesday, follows a proposal last year from experts and medical organisations to move obesity diagnosis beyond just body mass index (BMI), based on a person’s weight and height, to include body fat and broader health.

The study attempts to show what this new definition could mean for diagnosis levels, prevalence, and ultimately, treatment, for a condition the World Health Organization currently estimates affects more than one billion people globally.

Obesity can be a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, liver and kidney disease and cancer. The study suggests defining it as pre-clinical, when the condition is largely a risk factor, and clinical, when it is causing ill health.

Using data from almost 850,000 adults from China, Britain, the US and Spain, the study estimates that under the new framework, 1% to 3% of those defined as obese using BMI alone would not be, while another 5% to 9%, with higher body fat for example, would be diagnosed with the condition. Across a population, this could affect tens of millions of people.
The study’s senior author Francesco Rubino, professor and chair of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London, said the inaccuracy of BMI measurements was well-known.

“But we haven’t so far got a better system,” he said. That is what the new framework aims to do, he added, saying it could “provide a meaningful clinical characterisation of obesity that can inform care and policy.”

The new framework proposes measuring body fat, including by waist circumference, as well as BMI, and considering if a patient has any organ dysfunction linked to weight, like heart or liver problems, before making a diagnosis.

This means some people with high BMI alone would not be classed as having obesity. Those who have high body fat and high BMI would be diagnosed with “pre-clinical obesity”, and those who also have organ dysfunction would have “clinical obesity” – considered an active disease that would usually require more urgent treatment.
Under these criteria, only on average roughly 27% of people with obesity across the four studied countries have clinical obesity, the study estimated – representing around 8.5% of all adults.
